endings.text: You end the stroll at the corner of Lake and Wells, having looked at a store, the corner where a newspaper began and two public houses. Nothing was bought and no one was met; the evening is the outing's, the places are the town's.

You walk back west along Lake Street to the Sauganash and close the circuit where it began: two public houses, a store and the corner where a newspaper began. Nothing was bought and no one was met; the evening is the outing's, the places are the town's.

evidence.locator: Ch. XVII, 'Chicago in 1831' — the Wolf Point houses, Mark Beaubien's house just completed.
evidence.text: Wau-Bun describes the Sauganash in 1831 as 'a pretentious white two-story building, with bright-blue wooden shutters'.

evidence.locator: 10 June 1835 (Vol. II No. 8), p. 2, col. 5, the paragraph on the town's public houses (claim chicago_democrat_1835_06_10#c001). Transcription-mediated reading.
evidence.text: The Chicago Democrat of 10 June 1835 reported that the Sauganash had been repaired, fitted up and furnished with neatness and taste.

evidence.reasoning: The corner is given by the hotel chronology and the Chicago Landmark designation; the building's coordinate in the scene is the structure record's platted-corner derivation and carries the georeference's uncertainty of about 20 m.
evidence.text: The Sauganash stood at the south-east corner of Lake and Market Streets, on the east bank of the South Branch.

evidence.locator: 3 Dec 1833, p. 3, col. 4 (Peck’s standing card, run to 10 Dec 1834); 2 July 1834, p. 4, col. 4 (‘a full stock of fresh GOODS’). Transcription-mediated reading.
evidence.text: P. F. W. Peck advertised from the corner of LaSalle and South Water streets a stock of dry goods, hardware, groceries, crockery, boots and shoes, and hats.

evidence.reasoning: Andreas gives the corner. The structure record derives the coordinate from the modern West Wacker Drive / LaSalle intersection with a working uncertainty of about 20 m, so the stop calls the footprint our placement.
evidence.text: Peck's store stood at the south-west corner of South Water and LaSalle Streets; the corner is documented and the footprint's coordinate is derived.

evidence.locator: 26 Nov 1833 (Vol. I No. 1), the imprint; Andreas vol. 1, the press chapter on Calhoun’s office.
evidence.text: The Democrat’s first issue, 26 November 1833, gives its office as the building on the corner of South Water and Clark streets; John Calhoun printed it there.

evidence.locator: 20 May 1835 (Vol. II No. 5), p. 4, col. 6, the colophon (transcription lines 4177–4180). Transcription-mediated reading.
evidence.text: By 20 May 1835 the Democrat’s colophon gives the office as over Messrs. Jones & King’s hardware store, in South Water Street, so the corner is a former office on the scene date.

evidence.reasoning: Read off the issue numbers this project already cites from the same transcription: 20 May 1835 is Vol. II No. 5, 27 May No. 6, 10 June No. 8, 24 June No. 10 and 1 July No. 11. The numbers advance by one for every seven days, and 1 July 1835 fell on a Wednesday, so each of those dates is a Wednesday. No masthead statement of the paper's terms or day of issue has been read for this claim.
evidence.text: The Democrat came out once a week, on Wednesdays, and the number dated 1 July 1835 is No. 11 of its second volume.

evidence.locator: Andreas vol. 1, printed p. 633, the hotel chapter; the life of Mark Beaubien; DRLOIH hotel chronology, Exchange Coffee House entry.
evidence.text: Mark Beaubien built a new house on the north-west corner of Wells and Lake streets; in August 1834 Mr. and Mrs. Murphy took charge of it as a hotel, christened it the Exchange Coffee House, and remained until 1836.

The evening, the stroll, the route order, the looking from the street, the choice of where to end, both endings and the A Pleasant Circuit keepsake are invented connective narrative. The evening changes no lighting in the scene; no entertainment, meeting, purchase or dated event is claimed for it, no interior is opened and no one is met.

opening.text: An evening with nothing to do but look about. Begin at the Sauganash, pass a store and the corner where the town's newspaper began, then choose where to end. The evening is the outing's premise: the scene's light does not change and no dated event is claimed. Nothing to count or carry.

premise: A quiet circuit of the familiar streets: a shopfront, the corner where the town's newspaper began and two public houses, with nothing to count or carry.

stops.narrative: Set out from a public house's door.
stops.text: Begin at the Sauganash, on the corner of Lake and Market above the South Branch. Wau-Bun remembered it in 1831 as white and two-story, with bright-blue shutters; on 10 June 1835 the Democrat reported it repaired and newly fitted up. The evening and the stroll are our invention.

stops.narrative: A shopfront on the trading street.
stops.text: Over to the river and east along South Water Street to LaSalle and P. F. W. Peck's store. His card in the Democrat offered dry goods, hardware, groceries, crockery, boots and shoes, and hats. Look at the shopfront from the street; the corner is documented, the footprint is our placement.

One block east, at South Water and Clark, John Calhoun began printing the Chicago Democrat in 1833; by 20 May its office was over Jones & King's hardware on South Water Street. The paper came out weekly, and the number dated today is No. 11 of its second volume.

choices.consequence: Finish the circuit at the Murphys' corner of Lake and Wells.
choices.label: End at the Exchange

choices.consequence: West along Lake Street to the door you set out from.
choices.label: Walk back to the Sauganash

stops.narrative: A second public house, and a choice of where to stop.
stops.text: South to Lake Street and west to Wells, and the Exchange Coffee House, which Mark Beaubien built and Mr. and Mrs. Murphy have kept as a hotel since August 1834. No entertainment is claimed for tonight and none is invented. Choose where the evening ends.
